section: Instincts comparable with habits, but different in their origin
label: Instincts arise mainly by selection of accidental variations, not inherited habit
claim: Complex instincts originate chiefly through natural selection preserving and accumulating slight accidental variations of instinct; the inherited effects of habit play only a subordinate role.
quote: But I believe that the effects of habit are of quite subordinate importance to the effects of the natural selection of what may be called accidental variations of instincts
scope: instinctive behaviour of animals in a state of nature
measurable_quantities: heritability of behavioural traits
response of behaviour to artificial selection
transgenerational effect of learned behaviour on offspring behaviour
candidate_data: Behavioural quantitative-genetics studies and artificial-selection experiments on behaviour (e.g. Drosophila and rodent selection lines, Dryad experimental-evolution datasets).

section: Instincts graduated
label: Complex instincts are reached by gradations visible in related species
claim: Complex instincts are built up by slow, gradual steps, so gradations leading to them should be found among the instincts of related species in collateral lines of descent; instincts, like bodily organs, do not change by leaps.
quote: The canon of “Natura non facit saltum” applies with almost equal force to instincts as to bodily organs.
scope: complex instincts across related animal species
measurable_quantities: behavioural character states mapped on phylogenies
number of intermediate behavioural states among related species
candidate_data: Phylogenetic comparative analyses of behaviour using trees from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree combined with published behavioural trait compilations.

section: Aphides and ants
label: No instinct exists for the exclusive good of another species
claim: No animal performs an instinctive action solely for the benefit of another species, although each species takes advantage of the instincts of others.
quote: Although I do not believe that any animal in the world performs an action for the exclusive good of another of a distinct species, yet each species tries to take advantage of the instincts of others
scope: interspecific behavioural interactions among all animals, including mutualisms such as aphid–ant associations
measurable_quantities: fitness benefit to the actor in interspecific mutualisms
fitness costs and benefits of tending for aphids with and without ants
candidate_data: Field and experimental studies of ant–aphid and other mutualisms measuring partner fitness; meta-analyses of mutualism costs and benefits.

section: Instincts variable
label: Instincts vary within species in a state of nature
claim: Instincts vary within species under natural conditions, for example the migratory instinct varies in extent and direction and may be lost entirely, and nest construction varies between regions.
quote: instincts certainly do vary—for instance, the migratory instinct, both in extent and direction, and in its total loss.
scope: wild animals, especially birds (migration, nest building)
measurable_quantities: intraspecific variation in migratory distance and direction
proportion of resident versus migratory individuals
variation in nest form within species
candidate_data: Bird tracking data (Movebank), bird ringing recoveries, and nest-record schemes such as the BTO Nest Record Scheme.

section: Instincts variable
label: Fear of man is acquired slowly by animals exposed to human persecution
claim: Fear of humans is slowly acquired by animal populations persecuted by man, so animals on uninhabited islands are tame and heavily hunted large birds are wilder than small ones.
quote: But fear of man is slowly acquired, as I have elsewhere shown, by various animals inhabiting desert islands
scope: birds and other animals on islands and in regions with differing histories of human persecution
measurable_quantities: flight initiation distance
time since human colonisation
hunting pressure
body size
candidate_data: Published comparative datasets of bird flight initiation distances across islands and mainland regions combined with human-settlement history.

section: Domestic instincts, their origin
label: Domestic instincts arise from habit and from human selection of chance variations
claim: Under domestication new instincts have been acquired and natural instincts lost partly through inherited habit and partly through human selection, methodical or unconscious, of chance mental peculiarities, usually with both acting together.
quote: Hence, we may conclude, that domestic instincts have been acquired and natural instincts have been lost partly by habit, and partly by man selecting and accumulating during successive generations, peculiar mental habits and actions, which at first appeared from what we must in our ignorance call an accident.
scope: domestic animals (dogs, pigeons, fowls, rabbits)
measurable_quantities: heritability of breed-specific behaviours
behavioural differences between domestic breeds and wild ancestors
response to selection for tameness
candidate_data: Dog breed behavioural survey data (e.g. C-BARQ) linked to breed genomic data, and long-term fox tameness selection experiments.

section: Natural instincts of the cuckoo, ostrich, and parasitic bees
label: Cuckoo brood parasitism evolved from occasional laying in other birds’ nests
claim: The brood-parasitic instinct of the European cuckoo was generated by natural selection from an ancestor that built its own nest but occasionally laid eggs in other birds’ nests, where the fostered young fared better.
quote: By a continued process of this nature, I believe that the strange instinct of our cuckoo could be, and has been, generated.
scope: cuckoos and other brood-parasitic birds
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distribution of nest-building and parasitic habits in Cuculidae
frequency of facultative intraspecific or interspecific egg dumping in related taxa
candidate_data: Cuckoo phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) combined with published compilations of breeding habits for ancestral-state reconstruction.

section: Slave-making ants
label: Slave-making in ants arose from capturing pupae as food
claim: The slave-making instinct of ants arose when pupae of other species, originally collected as food, were reared and proved useful as workers, and natural selection strengthened this habit until some species became wholly dependent on slaves.
quote: the habit of collecting pupæ originally for food might by natural selection be strengthened and rendered permanent for the very different purpose of raising slaves.
scope: slave-making (dulotic) ants such as Formica sanguinea and Polyergus rufescens
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relationships of slave-making ants and their hosts
degree of dependence on slaves across species
predation on pupae of other ant species by non-slave-making ants
candidate_data: Ant phylogenies and natural-history records (AntWeb, AntWiki, Open Tree of Life) for comparative analysis of social parasitism.

section: Hive-bee, its cell-making instinct
label: Hive-bee comb building evolved by gradual modification of simpler bee instincts
claim: The cell-making instinct of the hive-bee was acquired through natural selection by slight successive modifications of simpler instincts, of the kind seen in a graded series from humble-bees through Melipona to the hive-bee.
quote: By such modifications of instincts in themselves not very wonderful,—hardly more wonderful than those which guide a bird to make its nest,—I believe that the hive-bee has acquired, through natural selection, her inimitable architectural powers.
scope: social bees (bumble-bees, stingless bees, honey-bees)
measurable_quantities: cell shape and regularity across bee taxa
phylogenetic position of comb-building lineages
cell packing geometry
candidate_data: Published comparative measurements of nest architecture in Apidae combined with bee phylogenies (Open Tree of Life).

section: Hive-bee, its cell-making instinct
label: Hive-bee cells form by bees sweeping equal spheres and building at intersections
claim: Hexagonal hive-bee cells result from many bees standing at equal distances from one another, each excavating equal spherical hollows, and building up or leaving unexcavated the planes where these spheres would intersect.
quote: The work of construction seems to be a sort of balance struck between many bees, all instinctively standing at the same relative distance from each other, all trying to sweep equal spheres, and then building up, or leaving ungnawed, the planes of intersection between these spheres.
scope: comb construction by the hive-bee (Apis mellifera)
measurable_quantities: shape of newly built versus mature cells
spacing of working bees
wall thickness and angles of cells
candidate_data: Imaging and micro-CT studies of honeybee comb construction and cell geometry, and experimental comb-building studies.

section: Hive-bee, its cell-making instinct
label: The hive-bee comb is maximally economical of wax
claim: The comb of the hive-bee is absolutely perfect in economising wax, so natural selection, driven by the saving of wax, could carry comb architecture no further.
quote: Beyond this stage of perfection in architecture, natural selection could not lead; for the comb of the hive-bee, as far as we can see, is absolutely perfect in economising wax.
scope: comb of the hive-bee (Apis)
measurable_quantities: wax per unit volume of storage
cell angles compared with mathematically optimal partitions
sugar consumed per unit wax secreted
candidate_data: Published geometric measurements of honeycomb cells and mathematical analyses of optimal space partitions; apicultural data on wax production costs.

section: Neuter or sterile insects
label: Selection on the family explains traits of sterile social-insect workers
claim: Traits of sterile workers in social insects can evolve because selection acts on the family: fertile parents whose colonies produce sterile members with a useful modification flourish and transmit the tendency to produce such members.
quote: selection may be applied to the family, as well as to the individual, and may thus gain the desired end.
scope: social insects with sterile castes (ants, bees, wasps, termites)
measurable_quantities: colony-level fitness in relation to worker traits
heritability of worker traits through queens and males
relatedness within colonies
candidate_data: Social-insect genomic and colony-fitness studies, including published relatedness estimates and caste-trait heritability data.

section: Neuter or sterile insects
label: Neuter insects of one nest should show graded structural differences
claim: If worker modifications spread gradually through selection of fertile parents, sterile workers of the same species in the same nest should sometimes show gradations of structure, and such gradations are in fact often found.
quote: On this view we ought occasionally to find neuter-insects of the same species, in the same nest, presenting gradations of structure; and this we do find, even often
scope: worker castes of ants and other social insects
measurable_quantities: within-nest distribution of worker size
allometry of head, jaw and ocelli among workers
frequency of intermediate morphs
candidate_data: Morphometric data on ant worker polymorphism from museum specimens (e.g. AntWeb imaging) and published allometry studies.

section: Neuter or sterile insects
label: Discrete worker castes arose by selection eliminating intermediate forms
claim: Distinct castes of sterile workers in one nest arose when a graduated series of workers was first formed and then selection on the fertile parents favoured production of the most useful extreme forms until intermediates were no longer produced.
quote: a graduated series having been first formed, as in the case of the driver ant, and then the extreme forms, from being the most useful to the community, having been produced in greater and greater numbers through the natural selection of the parents which generated them; until none with an intermediate structure were produced.
scope: ants with polymorphic worker castes
measurable_quantities: degree of caste discreteness across related species
phylogenetic order of continuous versus discrete worker polymorphism
candidate_data: Ant phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, AntWeb) combined with comparative data on worker polymorphism for ancestral-state reconstruction.

section: Summary
label: Allied species in distant regions retain nearly the same instincts
claim: Closely allied but distinct species living in distant parts of the world under different conditions often retain nearly the same instincts, which is explained by inheritance from a common ancestor.
quote: This theory is, also, strengthened by some few other facts in regard to instincts; as by that common case of closely allied, but certainly distinct, species, when inhabiting distant parts of the world and living under considerably different conditions of life, yet often retaining nearly the same instincts.
scope: allied animal species in different geographical regions (e.g. thrushes, wrens)
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic signal in behavioural traits
behavioural similarity versus environmental similarity among congeners
candidate_data: Phylogenetic signal analyses of behavioural traits (e.g. nest construction) using bird phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree.

section: Distinction between the sterility of first crosses and of hybrids
label: Sterility of first crosses differs from sterility of hybrids
claim: The sterility of first crosses between pure species, whose reproductive organs are perfect, is a different phenomenon from the sterility of their hybrids, whose reproductive organs are functionally impotent.
quote: Pure species have of course their organs of reproduction in a perfect condition, yet when intercrossed they produce either few or no offspring. Hybrids, on the other hand, have their reproductive organs functionally impotent
scope: plants and animals crossed between species
measurable_quantities: seed or offspring set in interspecific crosses
pollen or sperm viability in hybrids
candidate_data: Published plant and animal crossing studies measuring pre-zygotic and post-zygotic isolation separately (e.g. Coyne and Orr’s Drosophila compilations).

section: Sterility various in degree, not universal, affected by close interbreeding, removed by domestication
label: Some sterility in crosses between species is very general but not universal
claim: Some degree of sterility in first crosses between species and in their hybrids is an extremely general result, but it is not absolutely universal.
quote: Finally, looking to all the ascertained facts on the intercrossing of plants and animals, it may be concluded that some degree of sterility, both in first crosses and in hybrids,is an extremely general result; but that it cannot, under our present state of knowledge, be considered as absolutely universal.
scope: interspecific crosses in plants and animals
measurable_quantities: proportion of interspecific crosses showing reduced fertility
hybrid fertility relative to parental species
candidate_data: Compilations of reproductive isolation across species pairs (e.g. Coyne and Orr Drosophila data, plant crossing compilations) and hybrid zone studies.

section: Sterility various in degree, not universal, affected by close interbreeding, removed by domestication
label: Close interbreeding lowers fertility while occasional crossing raises it
claim: Close interbreeding lessens fertility, while an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases it; this explains much of the declining fertility of hybrids kept for successive generations.
quote: that close interbreeding lessens fertility, and, on the other hand, that an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases fertility
scope: plants and animals, including hybrids bred over several generations
measurable_quantities: fertility under inbreeding versus outbreeding
inbreeding depression coefficients
hybrid fertility across generations with and without inbreeding
candidate_data: Published meta-analyses of inbreeding depression in plants and animals and long-term pedigree datasets from zoos and livestock.

section: Sterility various in degree, not universal, affected by close interbreeding, removed by domestication
label: Hybrid sterility can be removed under domestication
claim: Because many domestic animals are believed to descend from two or more distinct species that are now fully fertile together, sterility between species is not indelible but can be removed by domestication.
quote: we must look at sterility, not as an indelible characteristic, but as one capable of being removed by domestication.
scope: domestic animals derived from several wild species (dogs, cattle)
measurable_quantities: number of wild ancestral species contributing to domestic forms
fertility of crosses between domestic forms of different wild origin
fertility of wild interspecific hybrids versus domestic descendants
candidate_data: Ancient and modern genomes of dogs, cattle and their wild relatives in GenBank/SRA documenting admixture, plus crossing records of zebu and taurine cattle.

section: Laws governing the sterility of hybrids
label: Cross fertility is largely governed by systematic affinity
claim: The fertility of first crosses between species and of their hybrids is largely, though not strictly, governed by systematic affinity, so that species of distinct families never produce hybrids while closely allied species generally cross easily.
quote: Now the fertility of first crosses between species, and of the hybrids produced from them, is largely governed by their systematic affinity.
scope: interspecific crosses in plants and animals
measurable_quantities: crossability and hybrid fertility versus phylogenetic or genetic distance between parent species
candidate_data: Compilations of reproductive isolation versus genetic distance (e.g. Coyne and Orr Drosophila data and analogous plant and bird datasets) with divergence times from TimeTree.

section: Laws governing the sterility of hybrids
label: Reciprocal crosses between the same two species often differ greatly in success
claim: The ease of crossing two species often differs greatly depending on which species is the father and which the mother, showing that crossing capacity depends on imperceptible differences confined to the reproductive system.
quote: There is often the widest possible difference in the facility of making reciprocal crosses.
scope: plants and animals, including seaweeds (Fucus) and close varieties
measurable_quantities: seed set or offspring number in each direction of reciprocal crosses
hybrid fertility from each reciprocal cross
candidate_data: Published plant crossing compilations reporting reciprocal-cross asymmetry in hybrid viability and fertility.

section: Laws governing the sterility of hybrids
label: Difficulty of first cross and sterility of hybrids correspond only loosely
claim: Species that are hard to cross generally produce very sterile hybrids, but the correspondence between the difficulty of a first cross and the sterility of the resulting hybrids is by no means strict.
quote: Hybrids from two species which are very difficult to cross, and which rarely produce any offspring, are generally very sterile; but the parallelism between the difficulty of making a first cross, and the sterility of the hybrids thus produced—two classes of facts which are generally confounded together—is by no means strict.
scope: interspecific crosses in plants and animals
measurable_quantities: crossing success of first crosses
fertility of resulting hybrids
correlation between the two across species pairs
candidate_data: Reproductive-isolation compilations recording both pre-zygotic and post-zygotic isolation for the same species pairs (e.g. Coyne and Orr Drosophila data).

section: Sterility not a special endowment, but incidental on other differences
label: Cross sterility is incidental on reproductive differences, not specially endowed
claim: The sterility of first crosses and of hybrids is not a quality specially endowed to keep species distinct but is incidental on unknown differences, chiefly in the reproductive systems, of the species crossed.
quote: The foregoing rules and facts, on the other hand, appear to me clearly to indicate that the sterility both of first crosses and of hybrids is simply incidental or dependent on unknown differences, chiefly in the reproductive systems, of the species which are crossed.
scope: all species capable of being crossed
measurable_quantities: accumulation of reproductive isolation with divergence time
evidence of direct selection for isolation versus by-product divergence
candidate_data: Comparative studies of the rate of accumulation of reproductive isolation with divergence time (TimeTree divergence estimates with crossing data) and genetic studies of hybrid incompatibility loci.

section: Causes of the sterility of first crosses and of hybrids
label: Early embryo death is a frequent cause of sterility in first crosses
claim: A very frequent cause of sterility in first crosses between species is the early death of the embryo, which may be exposed to unsuitable conditions within the mother or the egg or seed.
quote: the early death of the embryo is a very frequent cause of sterility in first crosses.
scope: interspecific first crosses, especially gallinaceous birds and plants
measurable_quantities: fertilisation rate versus hatching or germination rate in interspecific crosses
stage of embryonic mortality
candidate_data: Published bird and plant hybridisation studies recording fertilisation and embryo mortality separately (e.g. avian hybrid egg-viability studies, endosperm-failure studies in plants).

section: Causes of the sterility of first crosses and of hybrids
label: Hybrid sterility resembles sterility caused by unnatural conditions
claim: The sterility of hybrids closely resembles the sterility induced in pure species by unnatural conditions of life: in both cases the reproductive system is disturbed independently of general health, by disturbed conditions in one case and by two organisations compounded into one in the other.
quote: Thus we see that when organic beings are placed under new and unnatural conditions, and when hybrids are produced by the unnatural crossing of two species, the reproductive system, independently of the general state of health, is affected by sterility in a very similar manner.
scope: hybrids and pure species under captivity or cultivation
measurable_quantities: fertility of hybrids versus general vigour
fertility of captive or cultivated species versus wild conspecifics
sex-specific impairment of fertility
candidate_data: Zoo breeding records (e.g. Species360 ZIMS) for captive fertility and published hybrid fertility and vigour measurements.

section: Parallelism between the effects of changed conditions of life and crossing
label: Slight changes of conditions and slight crosses both increase vigour and fertility
claim: Slight changes in conditions of life benefit organisms, and crosses between slightly different members of the same species give vigour and fertility to offspring, whereas greater changes and wider crosses tend to cause sterility.
quote: Hence it seems that, on the one hand, slight changes in the conditions of life benefit all organic beings, and on the other hand, that slight crosses, that is crosses between the males and females of the same species which have varied and become slightly different, give vigour and fertility to the offspring.
scope: plants and animals generally
measurable_quantities: offspring fitness as a function of genetic distance between parents
fitness under small environmental changes versus constant conditions
candidate_data: Published studies of optimal outcrossing distance and heterosis versus outbreeding depression in plants and animals.

section: Fertility of varieties when crossed and of their mongrel offspring not universal
label: Fertility of crossed varieties is not universal nor a species criterion
claim: The fertility of varieties when crossed is very general but cannot be shown to be universal, so it does not form a fundamental distinction between varieties and species; some varieties, such as certain maize and Verbascum varieties, are partly sterile together.
quote: I do not think that the very general fertility of varieties can be proved to be of universal occurrence, or to form a fundamental distinction between varieties and species.
scope: natural and domestic varieties of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: seed set or offspring number in crosses between varieties of one species
fertility of mongrel offspring
candidate_data: Crop germplasm crossing records and studies of intraspecific reproductive isolation (e.g. maize gametophyte factor studies, intraspecific crossing in Arabidopsis).

section: Hybrids and mongrels compared independently of their fertility
label: Hybrids vary little in the first generation but greatly in later generations
claim: Hybrids are only slightly variable in the first generation but extremely variable in succeeding generations, because the reproductive system of the hybrids themselves is disturbed.
quote: The slight degree of variability in hybrids from the first cross or in the first generation, in contrast with their extreme variability in the succeeding generations, is a curious fact and deserves attention.
scope: plant and animal hybrids bred over several generations
measurable_quantities: phenotypic variance in first-generation versus later-generation hybrids
candidate_data: Published crossing experiments comparing trait variance in F1 and F2 or later hybrid generations in plants and animals.

section: Hybrids and mongrels compared independently of their fertility
label: Apart from fertility, offspring of crossed species and crossed varieties are alike
claim: Apart from fertility, the offspring of crossed species and of crossed varieties are closely similar in their variability, prepotency, reversion and resemblance to their parents.
quote: Laying aside the question of fertility and sterility, in all other respects there seems to be a general and close similarity in the offspring of crossed species, and of crossed varieties.
scope: hybrids between species and mongrels between varieties, in plants and animals
measurable_quantities: parental resemblance of offspring
variability across generations
rates of reversion in backcrosses
candidate_data: Published comparative crossing studies of inter- and intraspecific crosses in plants and animals.

section: Summary
label: No fundamental distinction exists between species and varieties
claim: The facts of hybridism do not oppose, and rather support, the view that there is no fundamental distinction between species and varieties.
quote: Finally, then, the facts briefly given in this chapter do not seem to me opposed to, but even rather to support the view, that there is no fundamental distinction between species and varieties.
scope: species and varieties of all organisms
candidate_data: none known
